questions.q: Which of these setup objects comes from Order Management specifically, not from earlier courses in the path?
questions.explain: Order orchestration rules — the sequence of steps an order follows — are new to Order Management, unlike chart of accounts, legal entity, or AR transaction types.

questions.q: Where is the customer master record (account and site) maintained?
options: It is the same customer record set up in Accounts Receivable, which Order Management reads
Order Management keeps its own separate customer list
It is entered fresh on every sales order
It is maintained only in General Ledger
questions.explain: Order Management reuses the same customer account/site record you already saw created in the Accounts Receivable course.

questions.q: What determines how an order will be priced?
options: An item assigned to a price list that Order Management references
questions.explain: Pricing depends on items being set up and assigned to a price list that Order Management uses to calculate the order's price.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is a common root cause of "the order won't invoice" support tickets?
options: A missing or misconfigured setup object somewhere in the chain of references
The order having too many lines
questions.explain: A sales order is a chain of references into setup; a missing link (price list, enabled item, transaction source) commonly breaks invoicing.

questions.q: Which setup governs how a customer's later payment will be recorded and applied?
questions.explain: Receipt classes and methods, covered in Accounts Receivable and Cash Management, govern how payments are recorded and applied.
